Base case + inductive step (assume true for n = k, prove for n = k + 1). Used for sums, divisibility, inequalities.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Proof — a core area of A-Level Maths.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Proof brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Proof.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Which proof technique is best for disproving 'all primes are odd'?
options: counterexample
induction
contradiction
direct proof

mcqs.q: Induction is most suited for statements about:
options: positive integers
real numbers in general
complex numbers only
irrational numbers
5/6 — find common denominators (3/6 + 2/6).
x^(1/2) means 1 divided by x squared.
1/6 — by multiplying the denominators only.
2/5 — by adding numerators and denominators separately.
4.6 — look at the second decimal (4), which is less than 5, so round down.
4.65, because rounding to 1 dp means cutting after the second decimal.
1/6 — by multiplying the denominators only.
4.7, because the 8 at the end rounds the 4 up to 5, which then rounds the 6 up to 7.
x^(1/2) means x divided by 2 — half of x.
4.65, because rounding to 1 dp means cutting after the second decimal.
x^(1/2) means 1 divided by x squared.
The square root of x (the positive root when x is positive).
